title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Suprapubic catheterization is an essential urological procedure used to manage urinary retention when urethral catheterization is contraindicated or not possible. This procedure also offers an alternative long-term urinary drainage option, potentially improving patient comfort and reducing the risk of some complications associated with urethral catheters. However, it carries its own risks, both at the time of insertion and in the longer term.

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This educational activity provides healthcare professionals with a comprehensive overview of the relevant anatomy, indications, contraindications, techniques, and potential complications of suprapubic catheterization. Effective treatment of patients with suprapubic catheters relies heavily on the interprofessional team, including urologists, emergency medicine clinicians, general practice clinicians, nurses, and allied healthcare professionals. Therefore, this activity also explores the essential role of the interprofessional team in treating patients with suprapubic catheters to improve outcomes and minimize the risk of complications.

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Introduction
content: Suprapubic catheterization is a procedure in which a drainage tube (catheter) is inserted into the urinary bladder through the lower abdominal wall just superior to the pubic symphysis. The procedure is typically performed in individuals who cannot void when urethral catheterization is contraindicated, not tolerated, or unsuccessful. Suprapubic catheterization offers an effective alternative route to drain the urinary bladder when other methods are not clinically feasible, appropriate, or tolerated. Compared with urethral catheters, suprapubic catheters are easier to change, available in a wide range of sizes, associated with fewer catheter-associated urinary tract infections, require antibiotics less often, and are generally considered more comfortable for men with long-term catheter requirements. [1] [2]

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Introduction
content: Alternatives to suprapubic catheterization include urethral catheterization, intermittent catheterization, urinary diversion, and percutaneous nephrostomy drainage. These specialized drainage catheters are typically placed either via a percutaneous or open approach, typically guided by cystoscopic or ultrasound imaging to minimize the risk of complications. [3] [4] [5]

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: The urinary bladder is a hollow, distensible, muscular organ of the urinary system. The bladder has 2 main roles—the temporary storage of urine at low pressure and the eventual muscular expulsion of urine from the body. The bladder may be divided into the apex (located superiorly), body (main part), fundus (base), and neck (the area that continues into the urethra). The bladder is situated predominantly in the extraperitoneal space in the pelvis, posterior to the pubic symphysis, although there is a small intraperitoneal portion involving the dome. Please see StatPearls' companion resources, " Anatomy, Abdomen and Pelvis: Bladder Detrusor Muscle ," " Physiology, Urination ," and " Bladder Rupture ," for further information.

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: The Retzius (prevesical space) lies anterior to the bladder and posterior to the pubic bone, containing the bladder neck and the urachal remnants. [6] The lateral borders of this avascular space include the pubic rami and the obturator internus muscles. [6] Inferiorly, it extends to the puboprostatic ligaments in men or the pubovesical ligaments in women. [6]

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: The bladder is superior to and supported by the pelvic floor and deep perineal muscles. The bladder's internal lining is folded into rugae, allowing it to expand substantially without increasing intravesical pressure as it fills with urine. The normal maximum capacity is about 500 mL in healthy adults. The detrusor is a smooth muscle layer of the muscular bladder wall that contracts during micturition, expelling urine from the bladder. Please see StatPearls' companion resources, " Anatomy, Abdomen and Pelvis: Bladder Detrusor Muscle ," and " Physiology, Urination ," for further information.

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: The lower abdominal wall, just above the pubic symphysis, consists of the linea alba in the midline, with the rectus abdominis muscles located adjacent bilaterally. Inferior to the arcuate line, the aponeuroses of the external oblique, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis muscles pass anterior to the rectus muscles, forming the anterior rectus sheath, with the transversalis fascia passing posteriorly. Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Anatomy, Abdomen and Pelvis: Abdominal Wall, " for further information.

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: Open access to the dome of the bladder and the placement of a suprapubic catheter require passage through these layers, the space of Retzius, and the bladder wall itself to reach the bladder lumen. Although suprapubic drainage tubes commonly exit via the midline, a paramedian approach through the rectus muscle may sometimes be acceptable or even preferred, depending on the patient's body habitus and individual anatomical considerations. Following initial suprapubic catheter insertion, an epithelialized tract is established between the bladder and the abdominal skin through the anterior abdominal wall; however, it takes approximately 6 to 8 weeks to mature fully. An acute inflammatory response occurs in the first few days, followed by a granulation phase, which stabilizes the tract's position and serves as a scaffold for epithelialization. Over the next 2 to 4 weeks, the tract gradually matures with the formation of an epithelial lining along its length. By 6 to 8 weeks, a fully epithelialized and stable tract is typically formed, allowing safe catheter changes without the need for reimaging or direct visualization.

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Indications
content: Suprapubic catheterization has both emergency and elective indications. Emergency indications include acute urinary retention, in which urethral catheterization is dangerous or not possible, and trauma (eg, pelvic fracture with suspected urethral injury). [7] Causes of acute urinary retention that may lead to suprapubic catheterization include benign prostatic hyperplasia, urethral strictures, pelvic trauma, genital malignancy, meatal stenosis, phimosis, and extrinsic compression of the bladder. In the elective setting, suprapubic catheterization may be indicated for long-term bladder drainage in patients who are unable to void due to chronic urinary retention or neurogenic bladder dysfunction, such as spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis, diabetic neuropathy, or detrusor failure. [7] [8] [9] [10]

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Indications
content: Suprapubic catheterization is also commonly used in patients with reduced hip and thigh mobility, in whom urethral catheter placement is challenging, in those who are unable to tolerate long-term urethral catheters due to discomfort, urethral erosion (leading to traumatic or erosive hypospadias), urinary incontinence leading to dermatitis, acute prostatitis, or recurrent catheter-associated bacterial infections. [7] [11] [12] [13] Patients with fecal incontinence may also benefit from a suprapubic catheter, as it is less likely to become contaminated with enteric organisms. [12] Any condition that makes urethral Foley catheter replacement uncomfortable for the patient or technically difficult to perform may serve as an indication for suprapubic catheter placement. [12] Suprapubic catheters may also be preferred in patients who are sexually active due to reduced interference with sexual function and to allow for temporary postoperative bladder drainage, such as after radical prostatectomy, incontinence surgery in women, and pelvic organ prolapse procedures in women. [12] [14] [15] [16] These catheters are also generally preferred by patients who use wheelchairs. [12]

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Contraindications
content: Contraindications to suprapubic cystostomy are relatively few and depend on the insertion technique. Percutaneous suprapubic catheterization is absolutely contraindicated in patients with a nondistended bladder because of the increased risk of injury to adjacent structures such as bowel and blood vessels. The procedure is also contraindicated in cases of suspected or confirmed bladder cancer or uncorrected coagulopathy. [7]

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Contraindications
content: Relative contraindications to suprapubic catheterization include active skin infection or cellulitis at the planned insertion site, ascites, osteomyelitis of the pubis, previous pelvic surgery, overlying surgical mesh, orthopedic hardware at the pubic symphysis, or a vascular graft in the suprapubic region. [7] [12] [17] Caution is warranted in patients with previous abdominal or pelvic surgery, as adhesions and altered anatomy increase the risk of bowel interposition between the bladder and the abdominal wall.

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Equipment
content: Equipment used for suprapubic catheter placement varies depending on whether the technique is open or percutaneous. Equipment for both techniques includes sterile gloves, a gown, sterile drapes, and an antiseptic solution for skin preparation. For catheter insertion, a needle, syringe, local anesthetic, a scalpel, a standard Foley catheter (typically 14-16 French), sterile water for balloon inflation, and a suture to secure the catheter are required. Sterile gauze and dressings may be used for aftercare.

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Equipment
content: Additional equipment for the open technique includes a small self-retaining retractor, such as a Weitlander retractor, to maintain wound exposure, along with surgical instruments for sharp dissection, such as forceps and Metzenbaum scissors. Conversely, for the percutaneous (Seldinger) technique, a large-bore needle for bladder puncture, a guidewire, and a catheter insertion sheath or peel-away introducer are required, which are often provided in commercially available kits; if not, a 0.035" guidewire can easily fit through an 18-gauge needle. [18] The percutaneous approach is often performed using a flexible cystoscope; therefore, associated monitoring equipment is required. Portable ultrasound may be used as an adjunct to localize the bladder, identify nearby structures, reduce the risk of inadvertent bowel injury, and confirm catheter placement.

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Equipment
content: For changing a suprapubic catheter in a patient with a mature tract, standard catheterization equipment is required, including sterile gloves and a gown, an antiseptic solution for skin preparation, and a sterile field to maintain asepsis. A syringe is necessary to deflate the balloon of the existing catheter, and sterile lubricant may be used to facilitate the insertion of the new catheter. A Foley catheter of appropriate size with a 5- to 10-mL balloon is used for replacement, and a syringe filled with sterile water is used to inflate the balloon once in place. Other equipment includes sterile gauze or dressing, a securement device, a bowl for safe disposal of the removed catheter, and personal protective equipment.

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Personnel
content: Suprapubic catheterization procedures are typically performed by urologists and surgeons specializing in the genitourinary system. Other clinicians who may perform this procedure include interventional radiologists, general surgeons, urogynecologists, gynecologists, emergency clinicians, and trauma surgeons.

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Preparation
content: Depending on the clinical scenario, suprapubic catheterization can be performed under either general or local anesthesia. The patient is positioned supine, with a slight degree of Trendelenburg tilt positioning to displace bowel loops away from the bladder and minimize the risk of bowel injury. If rigid cystoscopy is required, the patient should be placed in the dorsal lithotomy position. Flexible cystoscopy can easily be performed in the supine position.

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Preparation
content: The lower abdomen is shaved, prepped, and draped. If the technique involves entrance via the urethra, the genitals are prepped and draped accordingly. Preprocedural abdominal ultrasonography or computed tomography (CT) scan is helpful, particularly in patients with prior abdominal surgical procedures, to ensure there are no bowel loops between the distended bladder and the abdominal wall, where they can be inadvertently injured during suprapubic tube placement.

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Technique or Treatment
content: Several techniques for placing a suprapubic catheter are well described, including open techniques and percutaneous procedures, with numerous variations and hybrid methods.
contents: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Technique or Treatment. Several techniques for placing a suprapubic catheter are well described, including open techniques and percutaneous procedures, with numerous variations and hybrid methods.

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Technique or Treatment -- Filling the Bladder
content: Filling the bladder with fluid is recommended before suprapubic tube insertion. The use of diluted contrast allows for fluoroscopic or CT guidance. Bladder filling can be achieved physiologically (urinary retention), with a cystoscope, by fluid injection with a catheter-tipped syringe through an existing urethral Foley catheter, or through a percutaneously placed suprapubic needle with the tip in the bladder. A minimum volume of 350 mL is suggested. [19]

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Technique or Treatment -- Filling the Bladder
content: Bladder distention moves the anterior bladder wall closer to the skin surface, allows for direct palpation of the distended bladder, and displaces bowel loops superiorly and away from the expected course of the suprapubic tube. [20] Ideally, ultrasonography with color Doppler is used to evaluate the bladder and identify the position of any possible obstructing vascular structures or intervening bowel. [20]

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Technique or Treatment -- Open Cystotomy
content: Open cystotomy involves a small, typically transverse incision roughly 2 fingerbreadths superior to the pubic symphysis. General or regional anesthesia is typically required. The bladder is ideally filled before attempting suprapubic tube placement, which aids in its identification. The layers of the abdominal wall are traversed to access the preperitoneal space. The bladder is identified, and dissolvable stay stitches are placed on either side of the intended cystotomy. A small cystotomy is performed, and the drainage tube is placed under direct vision. The balloon is inflated, or the tube may be secured to the bladder with a dissolvable purse-string suture. The fascial layers and skin are then closed around the tube, which is finally secured to the skin with a temporary suture.

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Technique or Treatment -- The Trocar Technique
content: The trocar technique is frequently used, and the bladder must be distended to perform this procedure safely. [20] A puncture site is selected, typically midline 1 to 2 fingerbreadths above the pubic bone. Local anesthesia of the skin and the anticipated suprapubic tract is performed. A small skin incision is made, and a Kelly clamp is used to open the subcutaneous tissues. The trocar, with its obturator, is then inserted into the bladder by firmly pressing slightly inferiorly.

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Technique or Treatment -- The Trocar Technique
content: With the obturator removed, urine should drain from the proximal end of the trocar, and the position can also be confirmed by cystoscopy. The trocar should be advanced into the bladder sufficiently to allow the anchoring mechanism of the suprapubic catheter to be engaged. Once this is accomplished, the trocar is removed, leaving the suprapubic catheter in place. [20]

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Technique or Treatment -- The Trocar Technique
content: One disadvantage of this technique is the relatively small initial catheter size, but it can be exchanged later and enlarged. Trocar kits are available for direct puncture into the urinary bladder, but they can increase the risk of injury to adjacent organs, particularly after previous abdominal or pelvic surgery. Abdominal ultrasonography, fluoroscopy, or pelvic CT scans are recommended to confirm that no significant anatomical structures, such as bowel, have migrated into the surgical area.

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Technique or Treatment -- The Percutaneous (Seldinger) Technique
content: The percutaneous technique is also commonly used. [20] Adequate distention of the urinary bladder is imperative for this approach. Local anesthesia is administered, and a spinal needle with an obturator is placed percutaneously through the suprapubic area until it enters the bladder. The position is then confirmed by the outflow of urine through the needle after removal of its obturator. Simultaneous cystoscopic examination allows direct visualization of the puncture needle as it presses on the anterior bladder wall and eventually punctures through into the bladder, increasing the safety of the procedure. [20] Sterile saline with or without diluted contrast can be added to the bladder if necessary. Radiographic guidance is desirable but optional, as contrast can be added to better visualize the urinary bladder. A guidewire is then advanced through the needle into the urinary bladder (a 0.035-inch guidewire comfortably fits through an 18-gauge or larger-bore needle). [20]

The position is then confirmed by the outflow of urine through the needle after removal of its obturator. Simultaneous cystoscopic examination allows direct visualization of the puncture needle as it presses on the anterior bladder wall and eventually punctures through into the bladder, increasing the safety of the procedure. [20] Sterile saline with or without diluted contrast can be added to the bladder if necessary. Radiographic guidance is desirable but optional, as contrast can be added to better visualize the urinary bladder. A guidewire is then advanced through the needle into the urinary bladder (a 0.035-inch guidewire comfortably fits through an 18-gauge or larger-bore needle). [20]

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Technique or Treatment -- The Percutaneous (Seldinger) Technique
content: The tract is then dilated with mechanical or balloon dilators passed over the guidewire to a size sufficient to accommodate a pull-away sheath. [20] The sheath with its obturator is passed over the guidewire until the tip is in the bladder. The obturator is removed, leaving the guidewire in place. [20] The selected suprapubic catheter is then passed over the guidewire into the bladder through the access sheath, which is removed after the catheter balloon is inflated. The catheter is then secured. [20]

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Technique or Treatment -- The Blitz Technique
content: Modifying a Foley catheter to allow passage over a guidewire is known as the Blitz technique. [18] [21] [22] [23] The tip of a Foley catheter can be easily modified to fit over a 0.035" guidewire to facilitate placement into the bladder once a passage has been sufficiently dilated. This procedure can also be used for difficult urethral catheterizations once guidewire access has been achieved. Please see StatPearls' companion reference, " Difficult Foley Catheterization ," for further information.

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Technique or Treatment -- The Blitz Technique
content: Cystoscopic confirmation of suprapubic tube placement is recommended when feasible. [20] Turning the direction of the cannula slot superiorly (towards the umbilicus) can reduce the chances of inadvertently advancing the catheter into the prostatic urethra. [24] This technique is detailed in an American Urological Association Core Curriculum video from the University of Colorado.

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Technique or Treatment -- The Curved Lowsley Prostatic Tractor
content: A curved Lowsley prostatic tractor can be used for a modified approach. [18] [25] [26] Local, spinal, or general anesthesia may be used. This specialized instrument is passed through the urethra into the urinary bladder, a step that requires easy transurethral access. Upward pressure is applied, bringing the curved instrument tip and bladder dome close to the abdominal wall. The tip of the Lowsley retractor is easily palpable through the lower abdominal skin unless the patient is obese. [18] [25] [26] A suprapubic cutdown is then performed directly over the easily palpable Lowsley, exposing the closed retractor tip. [18] [25] [26] The Lowsley is opened, and the selected Foley catheter, typically a 20- or 22-French catheter, is then securely grasped by tightening the jaws of the Lowsley prostatic tractor over the catheter tip. [18] [25] [26] The Lowsley is then carefully pulled back into the bladder, pulling the catheter tip with it. Pushing the suprapubic tube shaft downwards during this insertion may be helpful.

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Technique or Treatment -- The Curved Lowsley Prostatic Tractor
content: The balloon on the suprapubic tube is inflated, and the catheter is released from the Lowsley by opening its jaws. [18] [25] [26] Once the Foley catheter is released, the jaws are then closed, and the Lowsley is gently removed. [18] [25] [26] Occasionally, the catheter tip is in the bladder, but the balloon is inflated just outside. Therefore, a cystoscopy is recommended after placement to ensure proper positioning. [18]

content: Technique selection depends on the availability of supplies and equipment, imaging availability, individual patient characteristics, anesthesia requirements, the urgency of the procedure, and clinician preference and experience. Once placed, the suprapubic tube can be replaced with sequentially larger catheters until the desired tube size is reached.

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Complications
content: As with many surgical procedures, complications may be categorized into intraoperative, early postoperative, and late postoperative groups. Intraoperative complications include hemorrhage, vascular injury, bowel injury, intraperitoneal violation, catheter misplacement, and failure to enter the bladder during the initial procedure. [8] [12] [29] [30] [31] The risk of bowel injury may be reduced with preoperative imaging and intraoperative ultrasonography. [32] Early postoperative complications include pain, hematuria, infection, catheter dislodgement, and urine leakage. Late postoperative complications include catheter blockage, infections, cystolithiasis (bladder stones), loss of tract, localized cellulitis or overgranulation of the stoma site, persistent leakage, and, rarely, squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder or suprapubic tract. [7] [8] [33]

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Complications
content: Loss of the suprapubic tract is a significant complication that can be largely avoided with proper planning during catheter changes and rapid replacement if the suprapubic tube is lost. [34] The suprapubic tract may begin to close within minutes of catheter removal, so it is imperative to ensure appropriate equipment is available for catheter changes. [33] [34] If a patient's suprapubic catheter becomes inadvertently dislodged or falls out, prompt medical attention and replacement are important to maintain tract patency and avoid the need for repeat procedures or reintervention. [34] Although the tract may remain open for up to 24 hours, it typically closes within a few hours. Therefore, immediate replacement of the catheter is required to avoid additional surgical procedures. Even replacing the catheter with a smaller one can help maintain the tract, as it can be enlarged later. [34]

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Complications
content: Painless, passive dilation of the suprapubic tract can be performed once the passage is mature, typically after 6 to 8 weeks. Dilation is performed by gently replacing the suprapubic tube with a Foley catheter that is 1 French size larger. This procedure can be repeated every 1 to 2 days with the next larger French catheter until the desired suprapubic tube size is achieved. [18] This method of passive dilation is simple and painless but requires frequent catheter changes. Attempting to replace the catheter before the suprapubic tract is mature can result in losing the tract and loss of bladder access. [18] Use of a guidewire can be helpful if the suprapubic tube needs to be replaced before the tract is fully mature. [18]

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Complications
content: In patients with a chronic obstruction, such as benign prostatic hyperplasia, decompression of the bladder can result in postobstructive diuresis. Postobstructive diuresis is defined as urine output greater than 200 mL/h for 2 or more consecutive hours or greater than 3000 mL over 24 hours. This brisk diuresis is a physiological response to the sudden relief of a chronic obstruction. Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Postobstructive Diuresis ," for further information. Individuals with a residual volume of greater than 1150 mL or elevated serum creatinine at the time of obstruction relief are at risk for this adverse effect. [35] Patients with immediate drainage of 1500 mL or more from a distended bladder are also at high risk for developing postobstructive diuresis, especially if their urinary retention was chronic. [35] Treatment of this condition generally involves fluid restriction. Please see StatPearls' companion reference, " Postobstructive Diuresis ," for further information. Other rare complications have been reported, including obstruction of the ureteric orifice by the catheter balloon, circumferential catheter-tip encrustation, and herniation of the bladder through the suprapubic tract. [19] [36] [37] [38] Finally, although not a surgical complication, patients may experience body image concerns. [39] [40]

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Clinical Significance
content: Suprapubic catheterization is an effective, well-established method of bladder drainage for patients in whom urethral catheterization is contraindicated, impossible, or undesirable and may be used in both emergent and elective settings. The procedure is beneficial for long-term management of chronic urinary retention, neurogenic bladder, or other conditions requiring long-term catheterization. [7] [8] [9] [12] Compared with urethral catheters, suprapubic catheters offer several potential advantages, including improved patient comfort, reduced risk of urethral complications (particularly in men), fewer catheter-associated urinary tract infections, the ability to use a larger tube size (less likely to become obstructed), easier daily maintenance, lower risk of accidental traumatic extraction, and less interference with sexual activity. [12] Furthermore, voiding trials can be performed by filling the bladder and clamping the suprapubic tube. Additionally, anatomical positioning can facilitate more convenient and comfortable catheter changes.

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Clinical Significance
content: Several studies have suggested that limiting genital contact with the catheter may decrease symptomatic infection rates and hospitalizations. [12] Results from a meta-analysis of 14 randomized controlled trials involving 1391 patients concluded that suprapubic or intermittent catheterization is associated with a lower rate of urinary tract infection when the duration of catheterization exceeds 5 days. [41] Other study findings have supported this lower infection risk, including one showing that nursing home residents with suprapubic catheters had fewer urinary tract infections, fewer hospitalizations, and less antibiotic use than those with long-term urethral catheters. However, nursing home residents with suprapubic catheters were more likely to be colonized by multidrug-resistant organisms. [1]

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Clinical Significance
content: In addition to fewer catheter-associated urinary tract infections, results from a Cochrane review found lower rates of asymptomatic bacteriuria and catheter-related pain with suprapubic tubes than with permanent urethral catheters. [11] However, urinary incontinence via the urethra can still occur despite the presence of a suprapubic catheter. The presence of urine on the skin is particularly concerning when skin breakdown from bladder incontinence is present. However, urethral catheterization can be a valuable safety measure if the suprapubic tube becomes blocked, minimizing bladder distension and reflux.

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Clinical Significance
content: Leakage around the suprapubic tube can also occur and generally indicates either tube blockage or bladder spasms. [18] Treatment of leakage may require catheter irrigation, tube exchange, treatment of an underlying urinary infection, or medication to reduce bladder spasms. [18] Switching to a larger French-size suprapubic tube or Foley balloon is not recommended, as these measures do not address the underlying cause of the leakage. [18]

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Clinical Significance
content: Suprapubic catheters can be placed for specific surgical procedures, and they can provide stable bladder drainage before and after complex urethral reconstructions. Additionally, they can be combined with a urethral catheter to provide high-flow continuous irrigation. Irrigation inflow can be instilled via the urethral catheter, and outflow via the suprapubic catheter. The larger-diameter tube, typically the suprapubic catheter, is used for drainage due to its improved outflow. In patients undergoing bladder, prostate, or urethral surgery, these tubes can be a valuable tool in maintaining adequate urinary drainage.

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Clinical Significance
content: Suprapubic catheters are not without risk and have several disadvantages. First, placement of a suprapubic tube requires a surgical procedure. Abdominal organs, such as the colon, can be injured during surgical placement. Urethral catheter replacement is still needed, and suprapubic catheterization does not eliminate the risk of catheter-associated urinary tract infections. If not placed correctly, the balloon of the suprapubic tube can migrate to the prostatic or even the pendulous urethra, causing pain and tissue damage when inflated. Finally, the suprapubic tube passage to the bladder often exits at the beltline, which can be uncomfortable for some patients.

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Suprapubic catheterization is a vital urological procedure that allows drainage of the bladder in patients who cannot safely undergo urethral catheterization. A suprapubic catheter also serves as a preferred long-term alternative route for many individuals requiring chronic bladder catheterization. The safe and effective management of suprapubic catheters requires an interprofessional team approach involving urologists, emergency care clinicians, general practice clinicians, nurses, and other healthcare professionals involved in the patient's care. Collaboration between team members is vital throughout the course of care, from procedural planning and catheter insertion to maintenance and complication management.

title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Patients with suprapubic catheters may have altered mental status due to neurological disorders or urinary tract infections; therefore, techniques to secure and prevent traumatic self-extraction have been described. Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Prevention of Inappropriate Self-Extraction of Foley Catheters ," for further information. Postprocedure, nursing staff members assume a central role in ongoing catheter care, monitoring for signs of leakage and dislodgment, and often performing the majority of catheter changes. Therefore, their assessment and knowledge of complications are critical. [13] [42]

content: Ongoing clinician and patient education, particularly regarding tract maturation, emergency reinsertion timelines, and infection control, can improve outcomes. title: Suprapubic Bladder Catheterization -- Nursing, Allied Health, and Interprofessional Team Interventions
content: Routine suprapubic tube replacement once the tract has matured is relatively straightforward. Although this procedure is often performed by nurses, caregivers should be trained and familiar with the technique. Permanent suprapubic tubes typically range from 18 to 26 French in size. Smaller sizes are more comfortable and flexible but tend to obstruct more often, so a 22-French tube is commonly used as a compromise. A 30-mL balloon is unnecessary, as it can be more irritating to the patient and cause more bladder spasms. A 5- to 10-mL balloon is generally sufficient to prevent catheter expulsion.

content: Suprapubic tubes should typically be changed every 4 weeks, but this interval ranges from 2 to 12 weeks. Regular irrigation is not routinely recommended but may be used to reduce obstruction caused by calcium phosphate debris. A 0.25% acetic acid solution can be used to help dissolve this material if it regularly obstructs the drainage tubes.
